title: Systemic Pathology candidate bank: Breast, Cardiovascular, Endocrine, Gastrointestinal and Renal Pathology

objectives.statement: Relate normal breast duct–lobular anatomy to common clinical presentations such as a mass or nipple discharge.
Differentiate inflammatory, non-proliferative, proliferative and stromal breast lesions using presentation and morphology.
Distinguish in-situ and invasive breast neoplasia, including characteristic ductal, lobular and special-type patterns.
Classify breast-cancer risk and prognostic factors without treating epidemiologic associations as deterministic.
Use circulatory consequences and structural defects to distinguish major heart-failure patterns and congenital shunts.
Analyze myocardial ischemia, infarction and hypertensive remodeling from symptoms, territories and complications.
Differentiate rheumatic, infective and sterile valvular lesions and apply valve-specific stenosis and regurgitation concepts.
Compare cardiomyopathies, pericardial disease and arterial pathology using mechanism and morphology.
Relate pituitary hormone excess, deficiency and posterior-pituitary release disorders to their clinical effects.
Distinguish thyroid and parathyroid hyperfunction and hypofunction using feedback, morphology and calcium effects.
Apply current diagnostic criteria and pathophysiology to type 1 and type 2 diabetes and their complications.
Differentiate adrenal cortical and medullary syndromes and recognize major multiple endocrine neoplasia patterns.
Differentiate major esophageal and gastric disorders using symptoms, mechanisms and complications.
Distinguish malabsorption syndromes and inflammatory bowel disorders using laboratory, histologic and distributional evidence.
Analyze appendicitis, diverticular disease and intestinal obstruction from anatomic and temporal clues.
Classify gastrointestinal polyps and cancers and interpret hereditary and screening-related evidence.
Relate filtration-barrier and juxtaglomerular anatomy to nephritic, nephrotic, azotemic and chronic kidney presentations.
Differentiate inflammatory glomerular disease and acute tubular injury using mechanism, urine findings and morphology.
Distinguish pyelonephritis, obstructive uropathy and major stone types from presentation and pathogenesis.
Differentiate inherited cystic kidney diseases, renal cell carcinoma and Wilms tumor using age, genetics and associated findings.

questions.stem: A pathologist describes a lesion arising from the functional unit formed by a terminal duct and its associated acini. Which structure is being referenced?
questions.explanation: The terminal duct–lobular unit (TDLU) is the functional unit of the breast and is the origin of many common epithelial lesions.

sources.title: Breast Pathology lecture deck
sources.locator: Slides 6–13, breast histology and terminal duct–lobular unit

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.rationale: This unit consists of the terminal duct and its lobular acini.
This is a small dilatation near the nipple rather than the functional duct–lobular unit.
This separates lobules and contains adipose and connective tissue.
This is an external structure and duct outlet region, not the TDLU.

questions.stem: A patient has intermittent bloody nipple discharge and a small subareolar lesion. Histology shows finger-like projections with fibrovascular cores lined by benign luminal and myoepithelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A large-duct intraductal papilloma commonly arises near the nipple and may present with bloody or serous discharge.
questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.rationale: The fibrovascular papillae and nipple discharge are characteristic.
Duct ectasia causes dilated ducts with inspissated secretions and chronic inflammation rather than true fibrovascular papillae.
A fibroadenoma is a mobile stromal and glandular mass and does not usually cause bloody discharge.
LCIS is usually an incidental microscopic finding and does not form a papillary subareolar lesion.

questions.stem: Three weeks after beginning breastfeeding, a patient develops fever and a painful erythematous breast after nipple fissuring. Which process best explains the presentation?
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial mastitis commonly occurs early in lactation when nipple cracks permit bacterial entry, often involving Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.rationale: The timing, nipple fissure, fever and painful erythema fit acute infection.
Duct ectasia generally affects older adults and produces dilated ducts and chronic inflammation.
Fat necrosis is usually linked to trauma or surgery and often presents as a painless mass.
Inflammatory carcinoma can mimic mastitis but is not explained by an acute postpartum fissure-associated infection.

questions.stem: A smoker develops a recurrent painful subareolar abscess and a fistulous opening at the areolar edge. Which initiating epithelial change is most likely?
questions.explanation: Periductal mastitis is associated with squamous metaplasia of major lactiferous ducts, keratin accumulation, duct rupture and granulomatous inflammation.
questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.text: Squamous metaplasia of a major lactiferous duct
options.rationale: Keratin accumulation and rupture produce the inflammatory abscess and fistula.

options.text: Apocrine metaplasia in a fibrocystic cyst
options.rationale: Apocrine cysts do not typically produce a recurrent subareolar fistula.
This is a clonal epithelial proliferation, not the initiating change in a subareolar abscess.

options.text: Loss of myoepithelial cells around a duct
options.rationale: Myoepithelial loss is a marker of invasion, not the smoking-associated initiating event.

questions.stem: Months after breast surgery, a patient develops a firm painless mass with skin retraction and calcification on imaging. Biopsy shows lipid-laden macrophages and fibrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fat necrosis follows trauma or surgery and can closely mimic carcinoma clinically and radiologically.
questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.rationale: The post-traumatic setting, macrophages, fibrosis and calcification are characteristic.

options.text: Invasive carcinoma of no special type
options.rationale: Carcinoma may retract skin but would show malignant epithelial invasion rather than a reparative fat-necrosis pattern.
A galactocele is a milk-filled ductal cyst during lactation.
A fibroadenoma is usually a well-circumscribed mobile mass without necrotic adipose and macrophages.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old has a rapidly enlarging breast mass. The lesion is large and only partly circumscribed; microscopy shows hypercellular stroma forming leaf-like projections around benign ducts. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: A phyllodes tumor occurs at an older age than a typical fibroadenoma and has hypercellular leaf-like stroma.
questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team

options.rationale: The age, rapid growth, hypercellular stroma and leaf-like architecture support phyllodes tumour.
Fibroadenomas are more typical in younger patients and usually have less cellular, well-circumscribed stroma.
Papillomas are intraductal fibrovascular lesions, not large leaf-forming stromal masses.
Mucinous carcinoma contains malignant cells in lakes of mucin, not benign ducts with leaf-like stroma.

questions.stem: Screening mammography detects clustered calcifications. Biopsy shows a clonal epithelial proliferation filling ducts, with central necrosis, but the basement membrane and an outer myoepithelial layer remain intact. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.explanation: Ductal carcinoma in situ is confined by the basement membrane; comedo-type DCIS may show central necrosis and calcification.

questions.stem: A breast biopsy shows small discohesive malignant cells infiltrating in single-file cords. Which molecular alteration most directly explains this architecture?

questions.stem: A clinician is explaining factors associated with breast-cancer risk. Select the findings that generally increase risk rather than reduce it.

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team
questions.sampleAnswer: Dilated cardiomyopathy has enlarged chambers and reduced systolic pump function, often with mural thrombi. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has marked, often asymmetric septal hypertrophy without dilation and may obstruct left-ventricular outflow or cause sudden death. Restrictive cardiomyopathy has relatively nondilated stiff ventricles with impaired diastolic filling, as in amyloidosis or endomyocardial fibrosis.
rubric: Correctly describes dilated cardiomyopathy as chamber dilation with predominant systolic dysfunction.
Correctly describes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as marked hypertrophy, often asymmetric, with impaired filling and possible outflow obstruction.
Correctly describes restrictive cardiomyopathy as stiff ventricles with impaired diastolic filling and relatively reduced chamber volume.
Provides at least one appropriate clinical or morphologic clue for each pattern.
Links structure to functional consequence rather than merely naming conditions.

questions.stem: Construct a concise mechanism-based comparison of Cushing disease, exogenous Cushing syndrome and primary adrenal insufficiency. Include the direction of cortisol and ACTH change, one characteristic clinical clue, and the feedback logic that produces the hormone pattern.
questions.explanation: A strong response separates pituitary ACTH excess, exogenous glucocorticoid suppression and primary adrenal failure rather than treating all cortisol disorders as a single syndrome.

questions.author: Optometry Study Hub authoring team
questions.sampleAnswer: Cushing disease is a pituitary ACTH-secreting adenoma, so ACTH and cortisol are elevated and patients may have central obesity, striae and hypertension. Exogenous glucocorticoid exposure produces Cushing syndrome with high glucocorticoid effect but suppressed endogenous ACTH and adrenal cortisol production through negative feedback. Primary adrenal insufficiency has low cortisol with compensatory high ACTH, producing fatigue, weight loss, hypotension and hyperpigmentation.
rubric: Identifies Cushing disease as pituitary ACTH excess with increased cortisol.
Explains that exogenous glucocorticoids suppress endogenous ACTH through negative feedback.
Identifies primary adrenal insufficiency as low cortisol with increased ACTH.
Provides at least one appropriate clinical clue for each state.
Uses feedback reasoning to explain, not merely list, the hormone directions.

questions.stem: A patient has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a distal “bird’s-beak.” Which disorder is most likely?
